Title: Imaging cells and nanoparticles using modulated optically computed phase microscopy
Text:
Imaging cells and nanoparticles 
using modulated optically 
computed phase microscopy
Xuan Liu1, Rupak Bhakta1, Emily Kryvorutsky2 & Yuanwei Zhang2
Nanoparticles (NPs) have been successfully used as drug delivery systems. To develop and optimize 
NP-based drug delivery systems, it is essential to understand the dynamics of cell-NP interactions. 
Quantitative phase imaging techniques enable label-free imaging and have the potential to reveal 
how cells interact with NPs. To measure the subtle motion at cellular and subcellular scales, it requires 
a high phase sensitivity and a high spatial resolution. However, phase imaging techniques are limited 
by an intrinsic tradeoff between sensitivity and resolution. To overcome the tradeoff, we develop 
a technology termed as modulated optically computed phase microscopy (M-OCPM) based on low 
coherence interferometry and optical computation. The key innovation of M-OCPM is to utilize optical 
computation that performs Fourier transform of the interferometric spectra, imposes temporal 
modulation on the interference signal, and circumvents the sensitivity-resolution tradeoff. We 
evaluated the performance of M-OCPM using various samples, and demonstrated its label-free imaging 
capability, high sensitivity (nanometer scale displacement sensitivity) and high resolution (~ 250 nm). 
Particularly, we imaged NPs along with cultured cells and showed different signal characteristics for 
NPs that were adhered to the cells or in the cell culture medium. Our results clearly demonstrated the 
feasibility of M-OCPM in studying cell-NP interactions.
As an emerging drug delivery approach, nanoparticles (NPs) have been successfully used in many medical 
treatments. The approved drugs with NP carriers include Doxil and Epaxal, and COVID-19 vaccines 1. To 
develop and optimize nanoparticle (NP)-based drug delivery systems, it is essential to understand the dynamics 
of cell-NP interactions 2,3. Optical microscopy plays a critical role in biomedical research and clinical diagnosis. 
Among various microscopic imaging techniques, quantitative phase microscopy is a powerful tool for the study 
of cell-NP interactions and the development of NP-based drug delivery systems 4–11.
To measure subtle optical path length variation at cellular and subcellular scales for the study of cell-NP 
interaction, it is desirable to achieve a high phase sensitivity and a high spatial resolution simultaneously. 
However, there is an intrinsic tradeoff between phase sensitivity and spatial resolution. As indicated by theories 
that model the information capacity of optical imaging systems 12,13, a higher phase sensitivity generally leads 
to a lower spatial resolution (and vice versa) due to the bounded information capacity of an optical imaging 
system. Many hardware and software methods have been developed to improve the image quality for microscopy 
techniques. However, most methods are dedicated to amplitude imaging techniques while these methods cannot 
be directly applied to phase imaging techniques. For example, to improve the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and 
detection sensitivity, the most straightforward method is to take multiple frames of measurement and average 
the result, effectively reconstructing the image with more signal photons. When shot noise dominates, the 
measurement sensitivity can be improved with more signal photons 14–18. However, this approach has limited 
effectiveness in phase imaging and can lead to reduced phase contrast, because the phase signal is affected by 
nanoscale mechanical displacement and phase wrapping artifacts. On the other hand, the spatial resolution of 
amplitude imaging can be improved by deconvolving the measurement with the known transfer function of 
the imaging system 19,20. However, it is challenging to improve the spatial resolution of phase imaging through 
deconvolution in post-processing, because the sample (such a cell) used in phase imaging is usually transparent 
and provides limited contrast in amplitude.
In this study, we develop a technology, modulated optically computed phase microscopy (M-OCPM) to 
achieve high resolution and high sensitivity in quantitative phase imaging. In M-OCPM, we utilize a novel 
optical computation strategy to optically compute the Fourier transform of the interferometric spectrum and 
impose temporal modulation to the interferometric term. With 3D data cube (x–y–k) acquired in M-OCPM,

we implement novel algorithms to obtain phase images with high resolution and high sensitivity. The key 
innovation of M-OCPM is to circumvent the sensitivity-resolution tradeoff by temporally modulating the 
interference signal through optical computation. The modulation does not rely on mechanical scanning. We 
evaluated the performance of the M-OCPM imaging platform using a variety of samples (resolution target, 
nanoparticles, and cells). We validated the high sensitivity and high resolution of M-OCPM by imaging 250 nm 
nanoparticles (NPs). M-OCPM demonstrated high phase sensitivity and revealed the subtle change of refractive 
index induced by individual NPs. M-OCPM also achieved high spatial resolution and resolved individual NPs 
that were adjacent to each other. We also obtained M-OCPM images showing how NPs adhered to cultured cells, 
which validated the potential of M-OCPM in studying cell-NP interaction and assisting the development of 
NP-based drug delivery systems. With its label-free imaging capability, high sensitivity and high resolution, we 
plan to use M-OCPM to study the dynamic interaction between cells and nanoparticles. Knowledge gained from 
the imaging study will lead to nanoparticle-based drug delivery systems with improved target ability, efficacy, 
and safety. Particularly, the imaging technique is valuable when designing and optimizing nano-carriers in the 
preclinical stage to study bio-distribution and nano-biological interface interaction 21,22.
Method
Principle of M-OCPM
The hardware of M-OCPM is based on optically computed phase microscopy (OCPM), a novel imaging platform 
developed in our laboratory. Figure 1a illustrates the schematic of the M-OCPM imaging system. Figure 1b 
summarizes how an M-OCPM phase image is obtained by processing the complex sample function with the 
hardware of M-OCPM and the computer algorithm.
The OCPM imaging platform has been described in our previous publications 23. Briefly, the imaging 
platform consists of a Michelson interferometer and an optical computation module 24. The interferometer uses 
an LED (455 nm) as the low-coherence light source. The reference arm and sample arm of the interferometer use 
a pair of water dipping lenses (40× Nikon CFI APO NIR Objective, NA = 0.8) to collect light reflected or scattered 
from the sample and reference arm. The output of the interferometer is interfaced with an optical computation 
module that has a diffraction grating (1200 lines/mm), a lens, and a reflective spatial light modulator (Holoeye 
LC-R 720). The spatial light modulator (SLM) projects sinusoidal patterns. Matlab 2023b (The MathWorks Inc) 
was used to implement algorithms for signal processing.

M-OCPM for high-resolution phase imaging
Here we discuss how M-OCPM achieves the highest spatial resolution that is allowed by the imaging optics. 
Generally, the phase refers to the location of the signal at a specific time and location within the cycle of a 
waveform. A waveform (1D, 2D, or 3D waveform in space and/or time) is needed for quantitative phase 
measurement. For techniques based on interferometry, the phase image is obtained by extracting the interference 
component from every pixel and quantifying signal variation that is induced by phase. M-OCPM preserves the 
imaging system’s spatial resolution, because it extracts the phase from a waveform defined in the time domain 
and does not affect the spatial bandwidth of the signal. As illustrated in Fig. 2a, each measurement taken in 
M-OCPM (Eq. (4) for continuous signal and Eq. (7) for discrete signal), is the superposition of the DC term, 
the amplitude term and the interference term that carries phase information. M-OCPM imposes temporal 
modulation on the interference term through optical computation and takes a series of measurements over time 
(Fig. 2b, left). By applying the Fourier transform to signal at individual pixels along the time dimension, the

Results
To demonstrate that M-OCPM achieves a higher SNR, we imaged a mirror and acquired iX,Y,T  (T = 0, 2, …, 
127), assuming the mirror was flat and had no phase features within a small region of interest. Figure 3a shows 
a single frame of measurement iX,Y,T =0  (DC subtracted) and the measurement is noisy. Figure 3b shows 1D 
signal obtained from the central column of iX,Y,0 (X = X0). Figure 3c shows the amplitude of IX,Y,Ω0 where 
IX,Y,Ω is the discrete Fourier transform of iX,Y,T  and Ω0 = Nω0∆t
2π
. Figure 3d shows 1D signal obtained from 
the central column of IX,Y,Ω0 (X = X0). Clearly, the SNR of amplitude data in Fig. 3c and d is higher than 
the SNR in Fig. 3a and b. This is because through Fourier transform the signals in different measurements 
superimpose in amplitude while the uncorrelated noise superimposes in intensity. With an improved SNR in 
amplitude measurement, the phase measurement is expected to achieve a higher SNR. To validate this, we varied 
the number of frames used to reconstruct IX,Y,Ω and estimated the phase that was the argument of IX,Y,Ω0. We 
calculated the standard deviation of the estimated phase (σϕ) from a region of interest (ROI with 17 by 17 pixels) 
at the center of the FOV. To accurately estimate the phase noise, we also eliminated smooth variation of phase 
data due to wavefront distortion by correcting the phase with a 2D polynomial. The results are shown in Fig. 3e. 
Clearly, σϕ decreases when more frames are involved to calculate the phase in M-OCPM. In Fig. 3e, we also 
show the fitting of experimental data with Eq. (12) where an additional constant term is introduced to account 
for the noise background. B1 obtained from the fitting is approximately: As N increases, the uncertainty in the 
estimation of the phase reduces, leading to improved SNR and phase sensitivity. The noise reaches a stable value 
(~ 0.053 rad), corresponding to the displacement sensitivity of approximately 2 nm.
To demonstrate the advantage of M-OCPM in both SNR and spatial resolution, we imaged a resolution target 
(1951 USAF resolution target). Figure 4a shows the phase image obtained by processing a snapshot measurement 
with Hilbert transformation. Figure 4b shows the M-OCPM image reconstructed from 128 modulated frames. 
Figure 4b resolves much finer structural details compared to Fig. 4a, and has a much lower noise level. To 
better illustrate the difference in spatial resolution, Fig. 4c and d show regions of interest (ROIs) containing the 
9th group elements of the resolution target. In Fig. 4c, OCPM without temporal modulation cannot resolve 
horizontal bars of the elements because of limited spatial resolution in the y dimension. In comparison, Fig. 4d 
clearly shows individual bars for all the elements of the 9th group.
To demonstrate that M-OCPM achieves the highest spatial resolution that is allowed by imaging optics, we 
imaged 250 nm nanoparticles (Absolute Mag™ PEG 300 and dextran coated 250 nm magnetic nanoparticles). 
To minimize aggregation of nanoparticles, we sonicated the nanoparticle solution before imaging. To reduce

Figure 6 shows the results of cellular imaging using M-OCPM. We used cultured mouse muscle myoblast 
C2C12 cells (in high glucose DEME, 10% FBS, 1% penicillin at 37 ºC 5% CO2) as the sample and took iX,Y,T  
(T = 0, 1, 2, …, 127). Figure 6a shows the phase image reconstructed by applying Hilbert transformation to a 
snapshot measurement. Figure 6a appears noisy and is affected by phase wrapping artifacts 29. We unwrapped 
the phase with a widely used algorithm described in Ref. 29. Figure 6b shows the unwrapped phase and Fig. 6c 
shows an ROI that has a cell. The image is blurry, and the contrast is low. For comparison, Fig. 6d shows the 
M-OCPM image. Figure 6d shows a higher SNR than Fig. 6a. Nevertheless, phase wrapping artifacts exist. After 
unwrapping, Fig. 6e shows individual cells that have morphology consistent with published results. Figure 6f 
shows the ROI in which the cell body and cell nucleus are clearly visible 30. Results in Figure 6d–f demonstrate 
that M-OCPM achieves a high spatial resolution to resolve subcellular structures and achieves a high phase 
sensitivity to reveal subtle changes in the phase.
To demonstrate the potential of M-OCPM in studying the interaction between NPs and cells, we introduced 
NPs to the petri dish with C2C12 cells and conducted imaging experiments. Before taking measurements, we 
waited for more than 15 min to allow the NPs to reach the bottom of the petri dish or adhere to the cells. 
Figure 7a shows the M-OCPM phase image reconstructed by taking 128 modulated measurements. In the phase 
image, NPs correspond to regions with large local variations of phase signal. We also show the amplitude of 
M-OCPM image in Fig. 7b where NPs correspond to regions with reduced amplitude signal because of reduced 
light reflectivity. Figure 7c shows the overlay of phase and amplitude image, which allows better visualization 
of both phase and amplitude features. In Fig. 7c, the phase data is used as the Hue channel and the inverted 
amplitude data is used as the value channel with an HSV color map (saturation = 0.8 for all the pixels). We 
selected a region of interest (ROI1) with one NP adhered to the cell membrane (red arrow) and another region 
of interest (ROI2) with a cluster of NPs in close proximity to the cell (green arrow). Figure 7d–f show phase, 
amplitude and overlay image for ROI1. Figure 7g–i show phase, amplitude and overlay image for ROI2. The NP 
in Fig. 7d–f can be more visualized than NPs in Fig. 7g–i. This is because an NP adhered to the cell (Fig. 7d–f) 
does not move freely. M-OCPM allows high-contrast imaging of adhered NPs that are not affected by motion 
induced signal degradation. On the other hand, NPs that are not adhered to the cell (Fig. 7g–i) undergo random 
motion such as Brownian motion, leading to a sub-optimal imaging outcome. By assessing the temporal 
characteristics of M-OCPM signal, it is feasible to determine the adhesion status of an NP, which is highly 
significant in understanding the interaction between NPs and cells.
Conclusion and discussion
In this study, we validated the performance of the M-OCPM imaging platform using various samples (resolution 
target, nanoparticles, and cells). We also obtained M-OCPM images showing how nanoparticles (NPs) adhered 
to cultured cells, which demonstrated the potential of M-OCPM in studying cell-NP interaction. With its 
label-free imaging capability, high sensitivity (nanometer scale displacement sensitivity) and high resolution

(~ 250  nm), M-OCPM has great potential in developing and optimizing nanoparticle-based drug delivery 
systems. In recent years, quantitative phase imaging has made substantial progress, and our approach represents 
the effort in achieving high sensitivity and sub micrometer resolution. Effort has been made in achieving high 
sensitivity in mid-infrared (MIR) phase imaging. Researchers demonstrated QPI with an expanded dynamic 
range, with a combination of wavefront shaping and dark-field QPI techniques 32. In a different study, researchers 
developed a MIR QPI system with two orders-of-magnitude higher signal-to-noise ratio with a homemade 
nanosecond MIR optical parametric oscillator and a high full-well-capacity image sensor 33. In a recent study, 
the Kramers–Kronig relations in digital holography were investigated to achieve high space-bandwidth product 
(SBP) imaging, demonstrating a complex amplitude image that can surpass the SBP of a bright-field image 34. We 
may incorporate similar approaches to improve our imaging capabilities in the future.
M-OCPM achieves high sensitivity and high resolution at the cost of the temporal resolution of the imaging 
system. By reconstructing one phase image using N modulated measurements, the temporal resolution of 
M-OCPM is reduced by a factor of N. When the temporal dimension is considered, the information capacity of 
an optical system can be expressed as Ninfo ∝ (2LzBz + 1)(2LyBy + 1)(2LxBx + 1)(2LTBT + 1)log(1 + SNR), where Lx, 
Ly and Lz are imaging ranges in x, y, and z dimension, Bx, By and Bz are spatial bandwidth in x, y, and z dimension, 
LT is the observation time range, and BT is the system’s temporal bandwidth. For a given information capacity, the 
imaging system can gain spatial resolution (bandwidths in x, y, or z dimension) or SNR with a reduced temporal 
resolution, which is consistent with our experimental results. However, the effectiveness of M-OCPM approach 
requires a static sample with a complex reflectivity that is modeled as (x, y) ejϕ(x,y) and does not depend on 
time. If the measurement is affected by motion, phase images obtained from M-OCPM will have a suboptimal 
resolution or a suboptimal SNR. When NPs suspended in glycerin were imaged, an optimal reconstruction was 
achieved by taking 64 measurements to reconstruct the phase image. When the cells were imaged, a better image 
quality could be achieved with more measurements (128 frames). This is because the measurement was more 
affected by random motion for small NPs than cells adhered to the petri dish. Nevertheless, the change of signal 
contrast can also be quantified to analyze the motion.
Phase wrapping artifacts are universal for all the phase imaging modalities and can largely affect the 
interpretation of phase data. Various unwrapping methods have been developed. However, it remains challenging 
to recover the actual phase profile from a noisy measurement, where the signal may change abruptly due to 
phase wrapping artifacts or noise. With suppressed noise, M-OCPM allows more effective unwrapping and more 
accurate reconstruction of the phase profile.
M-OCPM is similar to quantitative phase microscopy techniques that rely on phase shifting. However, these 
techniques usually modulate the optical path length to introduce phase shifting and reconstruct the phase 
images with a few measurements. M-OCPM achieves temporal modulation through optical computation and 
can utilize many frames of measurement to achieve the desired SNR performance. M-OCPM relies on optical
